title: Kagyu
hook: the lineage of Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa

segments.voice: Yesterday, terma: teachings hidden on purpose, found by treasure-revealers when the time was right. Your line was hidden treasure. What turned up in the drawer or the old thread? Day one thousand two hundred eighty.

A scholar sits reading at a great monastery in India, with books stacked around him. A shadow falls across the page. An old woman, bent and ugly in the story, is standing over him. She asks whether he understands the words. He says yes, and she laughs with delight. She asks whether he understands the meaning. He says yes again, and she bursts into tears. You understand the words, she tells him, but not the meaning. The scholar is Naropa. He puts down his books and goes looking for a teacher. Today: Kagyu.
screen: `A SHADOW FALLS ACROSS THE PAGE.` → `THE WORDS, BUT NOT THE MEANING.` → `KAGYU.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Kagyu is often rendered the lineage of oral instruction, and some call it the whispered lineage. What matters is in the name: teaching passed by mouth, from a teacher to a student who is ready, one link at a time. Second, the Indian links. Tilopa, in the story, was a wild yogi with no monastery at all. Naropa, the scholar, found him and served him through a long run of hard and strange trials before Tilopa gave him the teaching. Tradition says Tilopa finally struck him on the head with a sandal, and Naropa woke up. Third, the bridge to Tibet. Marpa was a Tibetan farmer and family man, with a wife and a household, who crossed the mountains to India more than once to study with Naropa, carrying gold to offer and texts to bring home. He's remembered as Marpa the Translator. Fourth, the student no one would have picked. Milarepa, tradition says, did terrible harm as a young man, using sorcery to take revenge on relatives who had cheated his mother. Full of remorse, he came to Marpa, who set him to building a stone tower, then ordered him to tear it down, then to build another, and tear that down too. Only after that did Marpa teach him. Milarepa went into the mountains, lived in caves, and sang his teaching in songs that are still sung. A wild yogi, a scholar, a farmer, a man with a past. No two of them look alike. The lineage passes anyway, whispered from one to the next.
screen: `KAGYU: THE LINEAGE OF ORAL INSTRUCTION.` · `TILOPA AND NAROPA.` · `MARPA THE TRANSLATOR.` · `MILAREPA'S TOWERS.` · then, large: `THE WHISPERED LINEAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Choose a short line you know by heart: a saying, a verse, a phrase someone gave you. Say the words once, slowly, aloud or silently. Then set the words down, the way Naropa set down his books, and stay with what they point to, with no words at all, breath after breath. When the words come back and start repeating themselves, notice it, and return to the meaning underneath. The bell holds the time.
Kagyu. The Tibetan school of oral instruction, the lineage of Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa, passed from teacher to student. Today's word.
Your line: the whispered lineage. Today, pass on one thing you were taught, quietly, to one person who might need it. Day one thousand two hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Kagyu Buddhists trace their practice through Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa, receive teachings in person from a teacher, and sing Milarepa's songs.

original.note: Tibetan: kagyu, often rendered the lineage of oral instruction.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kagyu is the name of a place in Tibet.
what it means: a lineage of oral instruction, passed from Tilopa to Naropa to Marpa to Milarepa.
what a scholar hears: a chain of very different people: a wild yogi, a scholar, a farmer-translator and a man with a past.

notes: Gloss of Kagyu (bka' brgyud) as 'lineage of oral instruction' / 'whispered lineage': confirm.
Naropa's meeting with the old woman (a dakini in the tradition) is told from the hagiography; the monastery (Nalanda) is unnamed on purpose. Confirm the order of her laughing and weeping.
Tilopa striking Naropa with a sandal: given as tradition; confirm.
Naropa's trials are left uncounted (tradition often speaks of twelve) and Milarepa's towers uncounted, per the claims rule.
Marpa crossing to India 'more than once' and carrying gold: confirm.
Milarepa's youth (sorcery as revenge on relatives who cheated his mother) is told briefly; a Keeper may prefer more or less detail.
